planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or water and set transplants into fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost; place in bright indirect light or a few hours of morning sun so the yellow leaf veins stay crisp against the green blade, since deeper shade mutes the pattern and hot afternoon sun can scorch it.

directions: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or water and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost, positioning plants in bright indirect light or a few hours of gentle morning sun. 'Aureoreticulata' is a long-grown bloodleaf sport prized for red stems and rounded green leaves netted with bold yellow veining, a striking contrast to the solid wine-red foliage of the plain species form already common in bedding schemes. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich soil and pinch stem tips regularly to keep the habit dense and bushy rather than sprawling and thin. Take cuttings before frost to overwinter stock plants indoors as a houseplant, since it holds its color well under bright window light through winter.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or water and set out after the last frost into evenly moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; lindenii holds its narrow, pointed foliage more upright and tolerates more direct sun than broader-leaved bloodleaf cultivars without scorching.

directions: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or water and plant out after the last frost into evenly moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Linden's bloodleaf is a distinct, narrower-leaved bloodleaf grown for glossy, deep blood-red, pointed foliage traced with bright pink veins on upright red stems, giving it a finer, more pointed leaf texture than the rounder-leaved bloodleaf cultivars already grown as bedding foliage. It tolerates consistently damp soil better than most foliage annuals, even brief waterlogging, making it useful along pond edges or in rain gardens in warm climates. Pinch young stems to encourage branching and take cuttings in fall to overwinter as a houseplant north of zone 10.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Set rooted stem cuttings directly into saturated soil or shallow water at a pond margin, bog garden, or wet container after the last frost; reineckii wants full sun to bright light and constant moisture to develop its deepest red color and will grow with its base submerged.

directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings into saturated soil, shallow standing water, or a wet container after the last frost, in full sun to bright partial shade. Native to South American wetlands, Alternanthera reineckii produces narrow, lance-shaped leaves in shades of burgundy, pink, and bronze-red arranged in neat opposite pairs along soft stems, and it is best known as a foreground and midground stem plant in aquascaping but performs equally well as a marginal or bog-garden accent along warm-climate pond edges. Color saturates most fully under strong light and consistently wet roots; shade or drier soil shifts the foliage toward green. Pinch stem tips to keep growth compact and take cuttings before cold weather to overwinter indoors in an aquarium, paludarium, or bright windowsill container.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set transplants out once soil has warmed well past the last frost date, into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Cognac's rich bronze color and dense habit both develop best in consistent heat and strong light.

directions: Plant transplants in full sun in average, well-drained soil once the ground has warmed after the last frost. Cognac is a patented calico plant selection that arose as a branch mutation of the pink-splashed 'Party Time' and was fixed for uniform, rich purplish-bronze foliage instead of its parent's variegated pattern, giving a warm, solid color block useful for tying together brighter bedding schemes. It forms a dense, freely branching, low mound that holds its shape with only light shearing and shrugs off Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity better than many bronze-leaved bedding plants. Propagate by stem cuttings, since patented cultivars are reproduced clonally rather than from seed; take cuttings in late summer to carry stock plants through winter indoors.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Raspberry Rum Alternanthera (Pink and Bronze Joseph's Coat)

planting.note: Set transplants out once soil is warm and frost danger has passed, into average, well-drained soil in full sun; strong light and heat intensify the hot-pink leaf color and keep the mounding habit dense.

directions: Plant transplants in full sun in average, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed after the last frost. Raspberry Rum is a patented sport of the bronze-leaved 'Cognac' selected for its saturated hot-pink and brown bicolor foliage, forming a dense, mounding, outwardly spreading habit that stays more compact than the straight species form of calico plant already grown widely as an edging plant. Bred in part for improved resistance to leaf-spot problems that can trouble alternantheras in humid Southern summers, it holds vivid color and a full canopy through the worst Gulf Coast heat. Mass it as saturated pink bedding color or mix it into containers against silver or chartreuse companions, shearing lightly to maintain density, and propagate new stock only from stem cuttings.

planting.note: Divide established rhizome clumps or plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall into well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; flavida tolerates coastal humidity and sandy soils well and needs little care once its clump is established.

directions: Divide rhizome clumps or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Native to coastal grasslands of southern Mozambique and northern KwaZulu-Natal, Dietes flavida forms clumps of narrow, arching, blue-green strap leaves and sends up wiry stems bearing pale gold-yellow, iris-like flowers marked with bold orange-brown blotches at the base of each of the six petals, opening in flushes over many weeks like its better-known relatives. As with other dietes, do not cut down a flowering stem until it has stopped producing new buds, since each stem reblooms repeatedly at the same growing point. Once established it is thoroughly drought-tolerant and largely pest-free, making it a low-maintenance choice for xeriscape beds, medians, and native or pollinator-friendly plantings in zone 9-11 Gulf Coast gardens.
sources: Kew Science Plants of the World Online
